case.case_title: W. K. C. Perera v. Prof. Daya Edirisinghe and Others

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner, having satisfied the Rules and Examination Criteria for the Degree of Bachelor of Fine Arts, was entitled to the award of the Degree without discrimination under Article 12(1) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that she had fulfilled all the requirements under the applicable rules and regulations and was therefore entitled to be awarded the Degree of Bachelor of Fine Arts.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that 'Advanced Drawing' was a 'main subject' requiring a 'C' grade pass, and that the petitioner was weak in that subject, thus justifying withholding the Degree. They also argued there was no public duty to award the Degree and that the University had discretion to withhold it.
key_facts: The petitioner completed all examinations and obtained an average over 40% in the final exam held in 1990.
The Rules classified 'Advanced Drawing' as a 'common subject', not a 'main subject'.
The petitioner satisfied all requirements for an ordinary pass including obtaining 'C' passes in main subjects and History of the Arts.
The University and Institute are public bodies performing public functions using public funds.
There was a refusal by the University and Institute to award the Degree despite the petitioner meeting the criteria.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 12(1) guarantees equality and equal treatment even where rights are not granted by statute or regulation. The Rules and Examination Criteria, read with Article 12, confer a right on a duly qualified candidate to the award of the Degree and impose a duty on the University to award it without discrimination. The Court rejected the respondents' reclassification of 'Advanced Drawing' as a 'main subject' and found the Rules clear and unambiguous.
reasoning.application_to_facts: Since the petitioner met all the requirements under the Rules and Examination Criteria for an ordinary pass, and the University is a public body bound by Article 12, the refusal to award the Degree was unlawful. The Court found no reservation of discretion in the Rules allowing the University to withhold the Degree and held that any discretion would be subject to Article 12's equality guarantee.
principles_established: Article 12(1) ensures equality and equal treatment even absent statutory rights.
Rules and Examination Criteria confer enforceable rights on qualified candidates.
Public bodies have a duty to act without discrimination under Article 12.
Discretion to withhold degrees, if any, is subject to constitutional equality guarantees.
Clear and unambiguous rules must be applied as written without reinterpretation.
precedents_cited: Sannasgala v. University of Kelaniya (1991) 2 Sri LR 193

outcome.holding: The Court allowed the appeal, quashed the refusal to award the Degree, and ordered the University and Institute to award the Degree to the petitioner without discrimination, enforceable by writs of Certiorari and Mandamus.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Order of Certiorari quashing refusal to award Degree; Order of Mandamus directing award of Degree; Costs awarded to petitioner.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the Court's reasoning as it guaranteed the petitioner equality and equal protection under the law, thereby imposing a duty on the University to award the Degree without discrimination once the petitioner met the criteria.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: Article 12 of the Constitution ensures equality and equal treatment even where a right is not granted by common law, statute or regulation... the Rules and Examination Criteria, read with Article 12, confer a right on a duly qualified candidate to the award of the Degree and a duty on the University to award such degree without discrimination.
